item.title: Prince Harry's wife Meghan 'deeply distressed' by allegations about her father
item.description:
Prince Harry's wife Meghan 'deeply distressed' by allegations about her father
Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, said she was “deeply distressed” by allegations that a collection of child sexual abuse images had been found at her father’s former homeByDANICA KIRKA Associated PressOctober 23, 2026, 7:13 AM
LONDON -- Prince Harry’s wife, Meghan, said Friday she was “deeply distressed” by allegations that a collection of child sexual abuse images had been found at her father’s former home. She also revealed that a letter containing “troubling allegations” about him had been sent to London police in 2018.
Meghan, also known as the Duchess of Sussex, issued the statement after The Sun, a British tabloid newspaper, reported that her brother found the images while clearing out the home of their father, Thomas Markle Sr., in the Philippines.
“I am deeply distressed at the news that has come to light in the last 24 hours, and my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed,’’ Meghan said in a statement.
She also addressed the letter sent to the Metropolitan Police Service’s Royal and Specialist Protection unit, which later shared its contents with her.
“It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated. I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications’ distortion over the years, any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children was for one reason: to protect them.”
Meghan, an American citizen who starred in the U.S. television drama “Suits,” married Harry at Windsor Castle in 2018. They have two children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet.

item.title: Philippines announce bounty on senator wanted by the ICC
item.description:
Philippines announce bounty on senator wanted by the ICC
Philippine officials announce a bounty for the capture of Senator Ronald dela Rosa, who faces arrest by the International Criminal Court for alleged crimes against humanityByJIM GOMEZ Associated PressOctober 23, 2026, 6:40 AM
MANILA, Philippines -- Philippine officials announced a bounty Friday for the capture of a senator who has been ordered arrested by the International Criminal Court for an alleged crime against humanity in connection with deadly anti-drugs crackdowns.
The court alleges that Sen. Ronald dela Rosa, 64, was an “indirect co-conspirator” of former President Rodrigo Duterte, who was arrested last year and now faces trial for alleged crimes linked to the so-called war on drugs he waged while in office.
Dela Rosa last appeared in public when he went to the Philippine Senate briefly in May but fled after the international court in The Hague, Netherlands, made public a warrant for his arrest.
Dela Rosa was the first national police chief designated by Duterte to enforce the brutal crackdowns he launched after becoming president in 2016. After dela Rosa retired from the police force, he was appointed as a top prisons official before successfully running for a Senate seat in 2019.
Estimates of the death toll in the crackdown on drugs during Duterte’s presidential term vary, from the more than 6,000 reported by the national police to up to 30,000 claimed by human rights groups.
Duterte and dela Rosa denied authorizing extrajudicial killings.
The ICC warrant, originally issued confidentially in November last year, charged dela Rosa with murder of “no less than 32 persons” allegedly committed between July 2016 and April 2018.

ShareFollow ABC News on Google
PARIS -- One person was killed and four others were wounded when gunshots were fired from a vehicle in a Parisian suburb on Friday, French authorities said.
A suspect was arrested near the town of Trappes and taken into police custody, police said, adding that the motive remained unclear.
“All available resources of the security forces and judicial authorities have been fully mobilized,” French Prime minister Sébastien Lecornu said.

item.title: Rescuers search for survivors after deadly earthquake in China’s Tibet region
item.description:
Rescuers search for survivors after deadly earthquake in China’s Tibet region
Rescuers are combing through a remote Chinese region in Tibet after a magnitude 7 earthquake that killed at least 16 people, injured 54 and collapsed hundreds of homesByThe Associated PressOctober 23, 2026, 4:13 AM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
BEIJING -- Rescuers combed through a remote area in the Chinese region of Tibet on Friday after a magnitude 7 earthquake that killed at least 16 people, injuring 54 and collapsing hundreds of homes, according to Chinese state media.
The disaster struck Nagqu, a city north of Tibet’s capital Lhasa that's some 4,800 meters (5,249 yards) above sea level, on Thursday. At least 339 homes collapsed, and officials told journalists they were concerned about further building collapses from aftershocks, as well as casualties from rockslides.
Search and rescue efforts are complicated by the geography and low temperatures, officials said. As of Friday afternoon, rescuers had done three rounds of searches, going through each household, and each village, said Dunzhu, the acting mayor of Nagqu city, said in a press conference.
More than 5,000 people from three local counties were deployed for rescue efforts. Supplies including 2,000 prefabricated housing units, around 3,400 tents and 2,000 folding beds, as well as flashlights and winter clothing arrived in the region.
The U.S. Geological Survey said the quake occurred at 10:33 p.m. local time on Thursday, with its epicenter 191 kilometers (119 miles) east-northeast of Nagqu. It put the earthquake’s depth at 18 kilometers (11 miles).
The U.S. agency recorded at least seven aftershocks with magnitude between 4.3 and 5.2, all of them with a depth of 10 kilometers (6 miles), according to its website.

item.title: UN climate fund promises just $20 million for Nepal flood recovery
item.description:
UN climate fund promises just $20 million for Nepal flood recovery
Disaster-hit Nepal will receive $20 million from the United Nations to help the Himalayan country recover from the devastating floods that killed thousands and destroyed buildings, schools, roads and dams resulting in billions of dollars of damagesBySIBI ARASU Associated PressOctober 23, 2026, 4:05 AM
BENGALURU, India -- A United Nations climate fund has provisionally set aside $20 million to help Nepal recover from catastrophic flooding that killed more than 1,400 people, left thousands missing and caused billions of dollars in damage to homes, schools and hydropower dams in the Himalayan country and in China.
Nepalese government officials and climate policy experts welcomed the move, but said the $20 million represents only a fraction of the $4.7 billion the government estimates is needed for recovery and reconstruction.
“It’s a very small amount compared to what we lost,” said Maheshwar Dhakal, a senior official in Nepal’s climate and environment ministry. But Dhakal said that releasing the money sends a significant message: “This shows that the global community can take the right decision at the right time to help those who are most vulnerable to climate change.”
The government said it had received around $102 million from domestic and international donors as of the end of September. Dhakal said the government is working with neighboring countries like India and China, as well as multilateral development banks, to raise more of the money it needs for recovery.
The U.N. Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage approved the payout — the fund's first — at an emergency board meeting Thursday.
The fund is aimed at providing assistance to countries hit by climate change. item.title: Pope Leo XIV cancels Assisi trip on doctors' advice as he recovers from surgery
item.description:
Pope Leo XIV cancels Assisi trip on doctors' advice as he recovers from surgery
Pope Leo XIV will not travel to Assisi on Tuesday for a major interfaith peace gathering because he is continuing to recover from thoracic surgery he underwent last week, the Vatican said FridayByThe Associated PressOctober 23, 2026, 4:01 AM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
VATICAN CITY -- VATICAN CITY (AP) — Pope Leo XIV will miss a planned trip to Assisi next week on doctors’ orders as he continues recovering from thoracic surgery he underwent last Tuesday, the Vatican said Friday.
The pope had been due to attend an Oct. 27 gathering marking the 40th anniversary of St. John Paul II’s World Day of Prayer for Peace.
In a statement, the Vatican said Leo was advised not to travel “to facilitate his recovery” from the surgery. The pope will instead send a message to organizers, Christian and other religious leaders, and guests attending the event, titled “Disarmed and Disarming Peace.”
The Vatican said Leo wanted to express his closeness to participants and reaffirm his belief that the “spirit of Assisi,” dialogue and the search for words and gestures of peace remain valuable resources at a time of conflict.
The Assisi meeting commemorates the landmark interfaith peace gathering convened by St. John Paul II in 1986.

item.title: South Korea proposes military talks with North Korea to calm rising border tensions
item.description:
South Korea proposes military talks with North Korea to calm rising border tensions
South Korea has proposed military talks with North Korea to resolve border disputes and prevent accidental clashesByKIM TONG-HYUNG Associated PressOctober 23, 2026, 3:04 AM
Share
SEOUL, South Korea -- South Korea on Friday proposed military talks with North Korea to resolve disagreements about where their border lies and prevent accidental clashes in frontline areas, seeking to ease tensions after recent landmine blasts injured three South Korean soldiers.
It’s unclear whether North Korea will agree to talks. Authoritarian leader Kim Jong Un has taken a hard line toward Seoul and has suspended virtually all dialogue and cooperation with the South in recent years. Meanwhile, North Korea has been adding mines, barbed wire fences, tactical roads, anti-tank walls and other fortifications to what’s already one of the world’s most heavily armed borders.
South Korea’s military has said North Korean soldiers crossed the border’s military demarcation line 50 times this year during fortification work, and that it responded with warning shots and broadcasts.
The South’s military made a proposal for similar talks in November that was ignored by the North. Seoul has shown greater urgency to ease tensions after the Sept. 21 mine blasts at the border, which the South’s military concluded were caused by North Korean mines planted south of the military demarcation line.
“Our Ministry of National Defense officially proposes to North Korean authorities that South-North military talks be held to mutually confirm the exact location of the ground military demarcation line between the South and the North, discuss the restoration of military communication lines, and discuss measures to prevent accidental clashes in border areas,” Kim Hong-Cheol, South Korea's deputy minister for defense policy, said in a televised statement Friday.

item.title: Taiwan shuts schools and grounds flights as Typhoon Champi brushes by
item.description:
Taiwan shuts schools and grounds flights as Typhoon Champi brushes by
Taiwan shut down schools and offices and grounded hundreds of flights as Typhoon Champi began brushing by the islandByThe Associated PressOctober 23, 2026, 12:50 AM
Share
TAIPEI, Taiwan -- TAIPEI, Taiwan (AP) — Taiwan shut down schools and offices and grounded hundreds of flights as Typhoon Champi brushed by the island Friday, packing strong winds and torrential rains.
Champi peaked at 298 kph (185 mph) maximum sustained winds earlier this week but has weakened to 155 kph (96 mph) winds as it approached Taiwan from the southwest. Its center is forecast to remain offshore as it sweeps by the island's northeastern tip before turning north toward Japan's southwestern islands.
Taiwan’s Central Weather Administration urged residents in coastal areas to avoid outdoor activities and driving and be cautious of falling objects.
One person was killed Thursday after being swept by waves in Liuqiu, a small island off the southeastern coast of Taiwan’s main island, according to the fire department. Ninety-four others were injured in the storm.
Almost 1,300 people have been evacuated from vulnerable, mountainous areas, the government said.
All of Taiwan’s 262 domestic flights were cancelled along with 669 international flights, according to the transport ministry. High-speed rail services on the western coast were operating normally.
In southwestern Japan, the typhoon has injured one person, grounded flights and knocked out power.
On Miyako island, a woman in her 70s suffered a broken leg in the blowing wind, according to the Okinawa prefecture government.

item.title: New Zealand's military chief resigns after admitting to an inappropriate relationship
item.description:
New Zealand's military chief resigns after admitting to an inappropriate relationship
New Zealand's military chief, Air Marshal Tony Davies, has resigned after admitting to an inappropriate relationship while in a position of commandByCHARLOTTE GRAHAM-MCLAY Associated PressOctober 23, 2026, 12:42 AM
WELLINGTON, New Zealand -- The chief of New Zealand's military, Air Marshal Tony Davies, resigned Friday after admitting to an inappropriate relationship as a unit leader.
“I regret not disclosing this when I had the opportunity to do so,” Davies said in his statement. He didn't elaborate on the circumstances of the relationship or when it happened.
Davies joined the country’s Air Force in 1984 and became chief of the New Zealand Defence Force in 2024. The military said leadership was transitioning to its vice chief, Rear Admiral Mat Williams.
“The resignation is for personal reasons, and results from errors of judgement made by me in the past, for which I am taking responsibility," Davies said. “The errors of judgement were contrary to the values of the Defence Force.”
The military said in a statement that it wouldn't comment further. The matter has been referred to an independent inspector-general who investigates military conduct.

item.title: A Ukrainian soldier lost his sight in war. Now he hopes to see his children again
item.description:
A Ukrainian soldier lost his sight in war. Now he hopes to see his children again
Ukrainian soldier Mykola Kasiuk is hoping to regain some vision after a battlefield injury left him nearly blindBySAMYA KULLAB Associated PressOctober 23, 2026, 12:08 AM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
KYIV, Ukraine -- Mykola Kasiuk’s world plunged into near-total darkness when a land mine exploded on the battlefield with Russian troops.
The Ukrainian soldier lost an eye. He clings to hope that one day he will see with the other because he can still discern faint traces of light.
After two years and numerous operations, Kasiuk placed that hope with a visiting team of U.S. surgeons.
Kasiuk crossed himself as he lay on a hospital bed before a recent surgery in Kyiv, praying for one thing:
“I want to be able to see my children again.”
Russia’s war in Ukraine has left soldiers and civilians with devastating eye and facial injuries. But specialists who can repair the damage are scarce. Before the 2022 invasion, ophthalmic expertise in many Ukrainian hospitals rarely extended beyond basic procedures such as cataract surgery.
The U.S. surgeons treat complex cases while training Ukrainian doctors in oculoplastic surgery, from rebuilding damaged eye sockets to fitting artificial eyes.
Local doctors had told Kasiuk that his vision was lost and recommended removing his remaining eye.
But he refused.
“No, I won’t let them,” he told his wife. “This is my last hope.”
Kasiuk trained as a military cook, not an infantryman. Still, he was handed a rifle and sent into some of the fiercest fighting in eastern Ukraine.
His last visual memories are consumed by the war's brutality in the Donetsk region: fellow soldiers killed, houses reduced to rubble, dogs wandering through ruins.
He could hear Russian soldiers’ voices nearby. The smell of death, he said, was everywhere.

item.title: Photos show festival on Myanmar's Inle Lake after the end of monsoon
item.description:
A few days after the monsoon rains subside, Inle Lake, nestled among picturesque mountains, becomes the setting for one of Myanmar’s most important Buddhist festivals as sacred golden images glide across the water.
The 18-day Phaung Daw Oo Pagoda Festival is an annual celebration on the country’s second-largest freshwater lake in the southern part of Shan state, about 420 kilometers (260 miles) northeast of Yangon. During the festival, four revered Buddha images are carried aboard an ornate golden barge to 21 villages around the lake for people to pay homage to them.
Adorned with a golden figure of the mythical Karaweik bird at its bow, the barge is pulled by scores of wooden boats crewed by members of the Intha ethnic minority, who practice a unique style of rowing while standing with one leg wrapped around a single oar.
